doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, November 11, 2017 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Learning from experience instead of music school; protocol on the bandstand
summary: Gates says learning through sideman work and sitting in, as with Billy Mitchell, beats school; Rowe asks how students learn protocol from book-schooled teachers.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well I was going to ask you about sort of that if you had gone the route of Berklee School of Music, get out, meet somebody and start working, in other words, I’m sort of describing what happens today hopefully for people.
But I wonder if your attitude about the music would have been different.

I wouldn’t have known half of the stuff that I found out the best way, from experience. The experience is the best teacher. The tuition is very high. Yeah. But it’s worth it ‘cause if they pluck you out of a music school, you might know how to play or execute, and then they make you leader. Well you don’t even know how to be a sideman. How can you be a leader if you’ve never been a sideman? And if you’ve never worked for a good leader and a bad leader, how do you know what it is to be a good leader? If you’ve never been taken care of by a good leader how do you know how to take care of your guys. To get them paid, to get them fed, to get them accommodated, or whatever. Yeah, “You take care of this, I’m busy.” No, no, no, no. That’s your responsibility if you’re the leader, in my mind. But I look at it, I mean I’m all wrong man. I’m looking at it the way it used to be. I thought that you learn your craft and then you work on it, and you learn it while you’re working on it, and you amass a repertoire and you learn about protocol and you learn how to work in what Lenny Bruce used to call “toilets.” Dumps. Dives. Where nobody’s listening. And maybe you can learn how to get them listening and have respect for the musicians that you are with on the bandstand, and have respect for the bandstand. I mean I’d never walk up on somebody’s bandstand and say, “Hey man, do you guys—” “What are you doing up here?” That’s the way it used to be. Now everything’s, “Oh sure baby, come on up.” You know? So I’m knocked out that I was able to find out from some of the people that I looked up to how to do it. Because I think that there is a certain protocol or je ne sais quoi or whatever you want to call it. The way to do it, there’s a way to do it. One could easily do something wrong with those guys. Like Billy Mitchell. I got to sit in at a gig, and I don’t know if we talked about this. Yeah I mean Billy Mitchell, “Yeah come by and sit in.” Billy Mitchell is running the band. Billy Mitchell from the Basie band? Yeah. Well you didn’t just, “Yeah baby everything’s fine, just come on up. Whatever you got is good.” No. “What do you got?” Before you get up here I want to know what you’re all about. I mean not in that way, but that’s the essence. What did Miles say? I could tell the way a cat walks if he can swing or not. They make judgement calls on you before you even open your mouth. And I think that was probably all right. Because they had been the route. And they know. Now, sure it’s fine, come on up. “How’d you sound?” “It sounded great man.” “Really?” “Yeah.” You know, like everybody drives a car. But not everybody is a good driver.

Well how the heck does a student these days learn that protocol? You had sort of mentioned that in today’s jazz education it seems that there are some people are now teaching who weren’t able to participate in that learning process. So you have mostly book-schooled professors now teaching another generation.
Yeah. Well it’s hard to teach somebody something that you don’t know about. I mean they don’t know about it. They don’t know about maybe getting kicked off the bandstand.
